lines: Multi-turn dialogue is the dominant mode of interaction with large language models (LLMs), and system prompts that specify task goals form the foundation of instruction following. As conversations grow longer, however, models progressively lose track of these goal specifications. \citet{dongre2026attention} quantified this degradation across 12 models: the Goal Accessibility Ratio (GAR), which measures how much attention the model allocates to goal tokens in the system prompt, declines by 27--48\% between early and mid-conversation turns. We replicate and extend this finding on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, observing a 70.8\% relative decline in GAR from 0.0418 at turn~1 to 0.0122 at mid-conversation. We attribute the steeper decline partly to our use of last-token GAR, which captures summary-position attention more sensitively than the all-token average of \citet{dongre2026attention}, and partly to Qwen-2.5-7B's stronger instruction-following fidelity in early turns. This attention decay represents a systematic failure of multi-turn models to maintain task coherence, and it grows worse with each additional turn.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

The failure traces to an incompatibility between teacher-forcing and GAR-family auxiliary losses, not to the gating architecture. NTP gradient pressure (7.5--14.7$\times$ the GAR magnitude) pushes gates toward identity (2--7\% attenuation), while inference-time steering ($\beta$\,=\,5) recovers GAR from 0.064 to 0.727, providing constructive evidence that attention misallocation is a proximal cause (\S\ref{subsec:steering}). Alternative hypotheses remain open; our evidence is consistent with exposure bias as the dominant factor but does not exclude alternatives. In particular, KV cache drift---the accumulation of model-generated key-value states whose statistics diverge from teacher-forced states---could compound the distributional mismatch beyond what prefix-level exposure bias alone predicts. Disentangling prefix-level and cache-level contributions requires interventions on cached representations, which we leave to future work. Split-softmax \citep{li2024measuring} and Rhea \citep{hong2025rhea} complement $\beta$-steering by restructuring attention computation at the architectural level, but cannot resolve exposure bias in auxiliary losses requiring retraining.

\paragraph{Scheduled sampling as training-time mitigation.} A preliminary experiment (single seed) applies scheduled sampling \citep{bengio2015scheduled}, mixing teacher-forced and model-generated contexts. AR GAR-ours increases from 0.016 to 0.318 (20$\times$), compressing the ${\sim}$31$\times$ gap to 1.57$\times$ with negligible PPL change (1.38 vs.\ 1.36), consistent with exposure bias as a primary driver. GAR-Dongre also rises (0.019$\to$0.353). On the $N$\,=\,50 evaluation, $\beta$\,=\,5 incurs 24\% PPL cost (1.43\,$\to$\,1.77); $\beta$\,=\,3 offers a more balanced tradeoff (+9\%); scheduled sampling incurs no fluency cost but requires retraining. A from-scratch second seed yields AR GAR\,=\,0.418 (gap 1.20$\times$), suggesting early scheduled sampling exposure may further compress the gap; systematic ablation is deferred.

Exploratory instruction retention analysis (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-ir}) shows +23.8\,pp content compliance at $\beta$\,=\,3, though statistical significance is marginal (McNemar $p$\,=\,0.077).

TRC analysis (\S\ref{subsec:mechanism-specificity}) confirms the mismatch targets attention routing without degrading representations. We scope claims to GAR losses on Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B; magnitude imbalance \citep{chen2018gradnorm} and Nash equilibria \citep{navon2022nash} remain untested.

The failure traces to an incompatibility between teacher-forcing and GAR-family auxiliary losses, not to the gating architecture. NTP gradient pressure (7.5--14.7$\times$ the GAR magnitude) pushes gates toward identity (2--7\% attenuation), while inference-time steering ($\beta$\,=\,5) recovers GAR from 0.064 to 0.727, providing constructive evidence that attention misallocation is a proximal cause (\S\ref{subsec:steering}). Alternative hypotheses remain open; our evidence is consistent with exposure bias as the dominant factor but does not exclude alternatives. In particular, KV cache drift---accumulation of model-generated key-value states diverging from teacher-forced statistics---could compound the mismatch; disentangling prefix-level and cache-level contributions is left to future work. Split-softmax \citep{li2024measuring} and Rhea \citep{hong2025rhea} complement $\beta$-steering by restructuring attention computation at the architectural level, but cannot resolve exposure bias in auxiliary losses requiring retraining.

\paragraph{Scheduled sampling as training-time mitigation.} A preliminary experiment (single seed) applies scheduled sampling \citep{bengio2015scheduled}, mixing teacher-forced and model-generated contexts. AR GAR-ours increases from 0.016 to 0.318 (20$\times$), compressing the ${\sim}$31$\times$ gap to 1.57$\times$ with negligible PPL change (1.38 vs.\ 1.36), consistent with exposure bias as a primary driver. A from-scratch second seed yields AR GAR\,=\,0.418 (gap 1.20$\times$), suggesting early scheduled sampling exposure may further compress the gap; systematic ablation is deferred. Exploratory instruction retention analysis (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-ir}) shows +23.8\,pp compliance at $\beta$\,=\,3 (McNemar $p$\,=\,0.077).
